meeting_header: Date: 2027-03-03 | Start: 15:00 PT | Duration: 54m | Platform: Zoom | Attendees: Maya Singh (Redwood AE), Lucas Turner (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Aurelius CTO), Ethan Cole (Infra Lead), Sofia Martinez (Security), Daniel Lee (DevOps)
summary: Deep dive on Private VPC deployment networking for Redwood Private: covered PrivateLink vs Transit Gateway, egress/NAT patterns, subnet design, Route53 private hosted zones and split-horizon DNS, security groups/NACLs, routing, and operational concerns like audit logs and KMS. Discussed runtime implications including latency/throughput, KV cache locality, batching strategies, quantization tradeoffs, kernel selection, and a pilot/benchmark plan.
topics: Route53 private hosted zones and DNS resolution
Runtime performance: KV cache locality, batching, quantization, kernel selection
Benchmarking plan and pilot next steps
transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro, I'm Maya, AE at Redwood. Lucas is our SE. Could we do quick intros from Aurelius?
[00:10] Priya (Aurelius CTO): Yep, Priya here, CTO. Ethan runs infra, Sofia is security, Daniel is DevOps. Thanks for setting this up.
[00:20] Lucas (Redwood SE): Great, thanks. Agenda is networking for Private VPC — PrivateLink, NAT, subnets, DNS — and then we can tie that into runtime impacts like latency and KV cache. Does that sound right?
[00:30] Priya: Yes, perfect. High level we want Private VPC because of data residency and we prefer no internet egress for model inference.
[00:42] Ethan: To add, we have a Transit Gateway in place but wanna understand if PrivateLink is better for Redwood endpoints. Also curious about egress for model updates and telemetry.
[00:52] Lucas: Okay, good. I'll start with the high-level patterns. There are two common connectivity patterns for Redwood Private: interface endpoints (PrivateLink) for control/ingress, and Transit Gateway/VPC peering for large cross-VPC traffic. PrivateLink gives you an ENI-backed interface in your VPC so traffic never traverses the public internet; it's ideal for control-plane and API calls.
[01:18] Lucas: Transit Gateway is better when you have a lot of egress between VPCs or want L3 routing across many VPCs — higher throughput but more configuration. For model inference traffic, most customers use PrivateLink for API requests and keep model cache and runtime co-located in the same VPC or same peered network for low latency.
[01:36] Sofia (Security): When you say "co-located" — do you mean we should put the inference nodes inside our VPC or Redwood's managed VPC? We prefer customer-owned network.
[01:45] Lucas: For Redwood Private with VPC mode, we deploy runtime instances into your customer VPC or into a private tenant space connected via PrivateLink depending on the deployment option. Best latency is when KV cache and model runtime are in the same subnets/AZs as the client traffic. If you need strict isolation we can run in your VPC with our control plane using PrivateLink.
[02:02] Ethan: If runtime is in our VPC, what about updates and model pulls?
[02:07] Lucas: Right — model artifacts can be pulled via a secure egress path. Two options: 1) Allow restricted egress to S3 or our artifact repo via NAT Gateway with egress-only policy and tight security group rules; or 2) use a VPC endpoint for S3 and pre-stage artifacts. Pre-staging avoids egress entirely. For larger models we recommend pre-staging and using an internal HTTP server or S3 Gateway.
[02:32] Daniel (DevOps): For private DNS, how do we handle service discovery? We use Route53 private hosted zones right now. Split-horizon DNS is ok.
[02:41] Lucas: We support Route53 private hosted zones. Typical pattern: Redwood provides a private hosted zone and you associate it with your VPC, or you create entries in your existing private hosted zone that point at the PrivateLink ENI IPs. Split-horizon is common — resolve the Redwood API hostname to the interface endpoint IPs internally. We can also support conditional forwarding if you have an on-prem resolver.
[03:00] Priya: What about TLS certs and mTLS? We require mTLS for control plane.
[03:06] Maya: We support TLS and customer-managed certs via ACM or customer-provided certs. For mTLS we have options: mutual TLS between runtime and control plane is available for Dedicated/Private deployments.
[03:17] Lucas: We can configure clients to present certs; Redwood's control plane enforces mTLS for API calls when enabled. For service-to-service, we recommend a short-lived cert exchange and can integrate with your internal CA if needed.
[03:27] Sofia: Audit logs and retention — we need 12 months of audit logs for compliance.
[03:31] Maya: We can ship audit logs to your S3 bucket or to your SIEM via an events stream. Retention is configurable; default is 90 days but we support long-term retention as an add-on. We'll include specifics in the security pack.
[03:45] Ethan: On throughput and latency — what are we looking at for p99 token latency if we host inside our VPC? We care about sub-100ms for short prompts.
[03:56] Lucas: There are multiple factors: model size, batching, KV cache locality, and network hop count. If runtime and clients are in the same AZ and KV cache is local (in-memory or local Redis), p99 token latency can be in the ~20-60ms range for smaller models. For larger LLMs, the model inference time dominates and you should expect higher single-token latencies but batching increases throughput.
[04:18] Lucas: Crucially, network RTTs to the control plane for streaming and token flushes can add overhead. That's why we recommend using PrivateLink and keeping control plane endpoints in the same region/AZ when possible.
[04:30] Priya: Can you explain KV cache locality? We have Redis clusters in each AZ. Is that enough?
[04:36] Lucas: Yes, that's the right idea. KV cache (the attention/KV cache for transformer decoding) benefits from being in-memory and co-located with the runtime. If your Redis cluster is cross-AZ, you may see added latency on cache hits. We recommend colocated in the same AZ or in-process KV cache where memory allows. Many customers run an in-process or local Redis instance per node for fastest retrieval.
[04:56] Daniel: If we run Redis per node, does Redwood support cache sharding or warm-up?
[05:01] Lucas: We have warm-up hooks and prefetch tooling. For cache warming, we can seed the KV cache based on expected prompt prefixes or use a persistent local cache snapshot. Sharding is handled at the runtime layer; the runtime can target local cache first and fall back to remote if a miss occurs.
[05:16] Sofia: Regarding NAT — our security policy says no internet egress except via approved NATs and egress proxies. How would Redwood's runtime get model updates?
[05:24] Lucas: Two paths: allow a controlled egress via your NAT to Redwood artifact endpoints, with strict egress rules (IP allowlist) and VPC endpoints for S3, OR pre-stage artifacts as I mentioned. If you want zero egress, pre-staging is the safest. Also we support a pull schedule that happens from inside your VPC via local processes.
[05:40] Priya: For larger gigs like 70B models, pre-staging means we need sufficient disk — what are typical sizes?
[05:47] Lucas: Model sizes vary — a 70B quantized model might be ~20-40GB depending on quantization. We provide recommended disk profiles per model; we'll share a sizing table in the follow-up doc. You can also use networked storage but local NVMe is preferred for latency.
[06:01] Ethan: What's Redwood's recommended subnet design? Public vs private subnets?
[06:06] Lucas: Typical layout: public subnets for bastion/management and NAT gateway, private subnets for runtime instances and caches. Put control-plane-facing ENIs in private subnets with security groups that only allow the control-port from your management subnets or PrivateLink ENIs. Use route tables per AZ to ensure traffic stays local. Avoid cross-AZ hops for latency-sensitive paths.
[06:28] Daniel: How about security groups and NACLs — any gotchas?
[06:31] Lucas: Security groups are stateful and usually sufficient. NACLs add stateless filtering but can complicate things; if you use them, ensure ephemeral port ranges are allowed for return traffic. Also: do not place overly restrictive NACLs on the subnet that has the PrivateLink ENI — it can block internal DNS or health checks.
[06:51] Priya: DNS TTLs — can we control them? We have a caching layer that respects TTLs; if PrivateLink ENI IPs change, we need low TTLs to re-resolve quickly.
[07:00] Lucas: You can set low TTLs on private hosted zone records. We typically recommend short TTLs for interface endpoints, like 60s, but be mindful of DNS query volume. We can also provide health-checked endpoints and recommend using SDK retries.
[07:15] Sofia: What about cross-account PrivateLink? Our VPC is in a separate AWS account from other teams' resources.
[07:22] Lucas: That's supported. You can allow cross-account VPC endpoints and we can accept endpoint connections from your account under the PrivateLink model. We'll need the account IDs and the service name for the endpoint. We can coordinate handshake steps in the follow-up.
[07:36] Ethan: On observability — we need per-request tracing and latency breakdowns — network vs runtime vs model.
[07:43] Maya: Redwood Console exposes per-route latency, token-level breakdowns, and traces. For Private deployments we can push traces to your tracing backend (Jaeger/OTel) or provide logs to S3. We can also include network-level tags in spans to distinguish network hops.
[07:58] Lucas: For benchmarking, we'll provide a template that measures: cold start, p50/p95/p99 token latency, throughput at various concurrency levels, cache hit vs miss, and quantized vs fp16 models. That will show network contribution to latency.
[08:14] Priya: Quantization — we plan to use int8. How does that impact throughput and accuracy?
[08:21] Lucas: Quantization to int8 reduces memory and increases throughput, often with small quality regressions depending on model and prompt. For many workflows int8 is a good tradeoff. We also support mixed precision (fp16) and custom quantization profiles; we can run A/B evals to check regression on your prompts.
[08:37] Priya: Can quantized models be served from the same runtime?
[08:40] Lucas: Yes, the runtime supports multiple model formats. You can pin routes to different model variants and do rollouts. Runtime will select kernels optimized for quantized ops.
[08:49] Daniel: About autoscaling — we need predictable throughput. How do you handle cold starts?
[08:55] Maya: We support warm pool instances and pre-warmed capacity for Dedicated/Private. Autoscaling is policy-driven and can be based on queue length or latency SLOs. For deterministic performance we recommend reserved capacity or a warm pool for predictable baseline throughput.
[09:10] Lucas: Cold starts happen when a model isn't resident; we mitigate with pre-loading and warm pools. For very large models, pre-loading increases infra cost but reduces cold-start latency. We'll help size the warm pool for your expected workload.
[09:22] Ethan: For networking, are we able to route traffic through our ASA or proxy? We have an egress proxy that enforces DLP.
[09:29] Lucas: Yes, you can route outbound connections via your proxy. For PrivateLink ingress no egress is needed, but for artifact pulls or telemetry you can route through your egress proxy. We'll need to whitelist Redwood artifact endpoints.
[09:40] Priya: Can you speak to Failover — if an AZ goes down?
[09:45] Lucas: We recommend multi-AZ deployments for runtime and cache. Use read-replicas or local caches per AZ. For PrivateLink, create interface endpoints in each AZ so the traffic stays local. Our routing supports fallback to a different region or model variant if necessary but that increases latency.
[10:01] Sofia: For keys and encryption, can we use our KMS and HSM?
[10:06] Maya: Yes, we support customer-managed KMS keys for at-rest encryption and can integrate with HSMs for key wrapping in some enterprise plans. We'll document the exact API for key rotation and access logs.
[10:17] Daniel: Is there any special configuration for IPv6?
[10:20] Lucas: We primarily support IPv4 for PrivateLink today; IPv6 support is on the roadmap but not generally available yet. If IPv6 is a hard requirement we'll log it and prioritize.
[10:30] Priya: Let's talk about pilot scope — we want to validate p99 < 150ms for our 1-2k QPS baseline on a 13B/70B mix. Realistic?
[10:41] Lucas: For 13B models colocated with in-process cache and proper batching you can get into low p99s. 70B models will be higher; with batching and quantization you can often hit throughput targets at slightly higher p99. The benchmark will tell. We'll plan the pilot to test these specific SLAs in your AZs.
[10:58] Ethan: Is there a recommended batching strategy? We have bursty traffic.
[11:02] Lucas: Redwood runtime supports adaptive batching. Policies can trade latency for throughput — max batch size and deadline scheduling. For bursty workloads, a small max-deadline (e.g., 50-100ms) can batch better without increasing p99 too much.
[11:16] Priya: Do you support prompt-level caching to reduce cost?
[11:19] Lucas: Yes, prefix caching and result caching are supported. We can cache deterministic outputs for certain routes and share caches across instances if locality allows. We'll help configure TTLs and invalidation.
[11:29] Sofia: How about regulatory concerns — data residency and audit chain?
[11:33] Maya: Redwood Private can be deployed to your region and on-prem if needed to satisfy residency. Audit chains can be exported to your SIEM and include per-request metadata. We also offer SOC 2 docs and can start an evidence collection for your compliance team.
[11:48] Priya: For the pilot timeline — what do you need from us?
[11:52] Maya: CIDR ranges, AZs, which models you'd like to test (13B/70B), a sample workload or prompt set for QoE regression, and a contact for security artifacts. We'll run a preliminary network test and provide the benchmark script.
[12:05] Lucas: We'll also need IAM access for S3 pre-staging if you choose that path, or allowed egress IPs if not.
[12:12] Ethan: Ok. On the native side, any limits on ENIs per AZ we should know?
[12:17] Lucas: Standard AWS ENI limits apply. If you anticipate a high number of interface endpoints we can coordinate and request limit increases in advance. We'll list expected ENI counts in the sizing doc.
[12:27] Priya: Anything about latency penalties for PrivateLink itself?
[12:31] Lucas: PrivateLink adds negligible latency — usually single-digit ms. The majority of latency is model compute and any cache miss network hops.
[12:39] Daniel: For logging and metrics, do you push Prometheus metrics?
[12:41] Maya: We can push Prometheus metrics to your pushgateway or expose metrics for scraping within your VPC. For higher security, we recommend pushing to your metrics ingestion endpoint.
[12:53] Priya: Let's open for questions from our infra/security folks.
[12:56] Sofia: A couple follow-ups: can audit logs be tamper-evident? We need chain-of-custody.
[13:02] Maya: We can enable write-once logs to S3 with Object Lock or ship logs to a SIEM that supports immutability. We'll include options in the security pack.
[13:12] Sofia: And for data-in-transit to model nodes, are you supporting in-path encryption with our internal TLS certs?
[13:18] Lucas: Yes, you can enable mTLS on all inbound connections and we can use your internal CA.
[13:23] Ethan: About the benchmark scripts — is there a standardized payload format?
[13:27] Lucas: We'll provide a k6/JMeter template that hits the Redwood API in streaming and non-streaming modes and captures token-level timings. We'll include a sample prompt set and instructions for CV/QA checks against your evaluation criteria.
[13:40] Priya: Excellent. Any known gotchas for Route53 private host zone association limits?
[13:45] Lucas: There are account-level limits on VPC associations; if you have many VPCs you might prefer conditional forwarding or Transit Gateway. We'll call out these limits.
[13:52] Daniel: For on-prem connectors, do you support AWS Direct Connect or VPN?
[13:57] Lucas: Yes, both. For low-latency on-prem we recommend Direct Connect, but VPN also works for proof-of-concept. We'll help with network diagrams for either option.
[14:08] Maya: Alright, quick recap and next steps then we'll close.
[14:11] Maya: Action items — I'll send security docs and the network diagram. Lucas will share benchmarking runbook and sizing. Ethan will provide CIDRs and AZs. Sofia will share compliance checklist.
[14:22] Priya: That works. We want the follow-up by next Friday.
[14:26] Maya: We'll hit those dates. Thanks everyone.
[14:30] Lucas: One last note — for pilot we recommend starting with 13B quantized, local KV cache, PrivateLink ENIs in the same AZ, and a small warm pool. We'll iterate on the 70B after the 13B baseline.
[14:45] Priya: Sounds good. End call.
[14:50] [call ended]
